title: NLP log pipeline
description: Producer, Kafka, the processor with its three detectors, MongoDB and the REST API of the NLP log pipeline: numbers from Prometheus, logs from Loki.

list.name: trace
list.label: Trace ID
list.description: The trace_id of one log line (for example the one the smoke test prints). Empty = all lines.

panels.title: Replay running (1 = yes)
panels.description: 1 while the producer pod is replaying the log file into Kafka, 0 when no replay is running. PromQL: sum(producer_sending)

panels.title: Log lines sent per second
panels.description: Log lines the producer hands to Kafka each second. The speed of a replay is LINES_PER_SECOND in config/pipeline-config.yaml. PromQL: sum(rate(producer_messages_sent_total[...]))

panels.title: Waiting in Kafka (lag)
panels.description: Log lines that are in Kafka and that the processor has not read yet. It grows while the producer is faster than the processor, which is busy whenever it scores a window. PromQL: sum(kafka_consumergroup_lag{group="processor"})

panels.title: Log lines stored per second
panels.description: Log lines the processor stored in MongoDB per second. PromQL: sum(rate(processor_messages_total[...]))

panels.title: Producer: log lines sent per second
panels.description: How fast the producer sends. It stays at the replay speed until the file is finished and then falls to zero (the pod is a Job: it is gone a little later).

panels.title: Producer waiting for Kafka (seconds per batch)
panels.description: Time the producer waits until Kafka has confirmed a batch of log lines. It grows when Kafka is the slow part.

panels.title: Consumer lag: log lines not read yet
panels.description: For the group processor: how many log lines are waiting in Kafka. Near zero = the processor keeps up. A line that keeps rising = it does not. During a replay it rises while the processor scores a large window and falls again afterwards. PromQL: kafka_consumergroup_lag{group="processor"}

panels.title: Processor: log lines per second
panels.description: What the processor reads from Kafka and stores in MongoDB each second, and how many of those lines carry an alert tag in the dataset (the ground truth: the detectors never see it).

targets.legendFormat: of which with an alert tag

panels.title: End to end: from send to stored (seconds)
panels.description: Time from the moment the producer sent a log line until it is stored in MongoDB, measured by the processor. When the lag grows, this grows with it.

panels.title: Processor waiting for MongoDB (seconds per write)
panels.description: Time that the three writes of one batch took (log lines, windows, replay status). If this rises, MongoDB is the bottleneck.

panels.title: Windows scored per minute
panels.description: A window is 5 minutes of the log (it moves on by 1 minute). The processor scores a window when a log line arrives that lies after the end of it. During a replay the log's own time runs far faster than the wall clock (the lines are sent at a fixed number per second, whatever time stamp they carry), so many windows are completed per minute.

panels.title: Windows flagged per minute, by detector
panels.description: How many of those windows each detector called anomalous: LogBERT (model A+), the rule-guided LLM (B3, its saved decisions) and the keyword rules (B4). The windows that really hold an alert line are in the table of  make results.

panels.title: LogBERT: seconds per window
panels.description: Time LogBERT needs to score one window (the keyword rules and the saved LLM decisions are lookups and take no measurable time). Long windows are cut into chunks and take longer; the NLP project reports 27 ms per window on average.

panels.title: Lines that needed care (per minute)
panels.description: Unseen = the line matches no template of the trained Drain parser (LogBERT counts such a key as missed). Too late = it arrived after every window that needed it was closed. Out of order = it arrived after a newer line but still found its window. Delivered twice = Kafka handed a message out again after a restart and the processor skipped it. All of these should be 0 or close to it in a normal replay.

panels.title: Log lines held in memory by open windows
panels.description: The processor keeps the lines of the windows that are not complete yet. A dense burst of the log makes this number large, and the memory of the pod grows with it (limit 1536 Mi; a window of 100,000 lines was measured at about 900 MB).

panels.title: Database writes per second
panels.description: Two views of the same thing: MongoDB's own count of write operations (from the MongoDB exporter) and what the processor says it stored. The processor writes every log line and every window as an 'upsert' (replace the document, or insert it if it is not there yet), which MongoDB counts as an update; the first start of MongoDB (creating the accounts) counts as inserts. The two lines should be close: MongoDB also counts the windows and the status of the replay. PromQL: mongodb_ss_opcounters{legacy_op_type=~"insert|update"}

targets.legendFormat: processor: log lines stored per second

panels.title: Open connections to MongoDB
panels.description: How many programs are connected to MongoDB right now (the processor, the REST API, the exporter).

panels.title: REST API: requests per second
panels.description: Requests answered per second (an average over the last 2 minutes), one line for each HTTP status that was answered recently: 200 = ok, 401 = no or wrong login, 404 = not found, 503 = the database did not answer. A status that nobody got has no line. At rest there is one line, 200, at about 0.3 requests per second: those are the health checks of Kubernetes itself.

panels.title: REST API: errors per second
panels.description: Server errors (red, 5xx: the API or the database failed) and client errors (orange, 4xx: wrong login, bad request). The red line is drawn on top, so a red line lying at 0 means that the server did not fail.

panels.title: REST API: how long an answer takes (seconds)
panels.description: Time from receiving a request to sending the answer.

panels.title: Is Prometheus reading it? (1 = yes)
panels.description: One bar per program that Prometheus reads the numbers of. DOWN means the last read failed (the pod is gone, restarting, or blocked). The producer has a bar only while a replay or a smoke test is running.

panels.title: Connected? (1 = yes)
panels.description: The processor says if it has loaded the models and is connected to Kafka and MongoDB; the MongoDB exporter says if it can reach MongoDB. A drop to 0 and back is a pod that was deleted and replaced.

targets.legendFormat: processor: models loaded, Kafka and MongoDB reachable

panels.title: Seconds since the last stored log line
panels.description: How old the newest stored log line is. It stays small while a replay runs and climbs when the pipeline is stuck. After a replay it climbs because nothing new arrives: that is normal (it is empty until the first line is stored).

targets.legendFormat: seconds since the last stored log line

panels.title: Producer send errors per second
panels.description: Messages that Kafka did not accept. Should be 0; it rises when Kafka is unreachable.

panels.title: Log lines per second, by program
panels.description: How many log lines Loki receives per second from each program, one line each (they are not stacked, so a line shows its own program only). If a program is missing here, its logs are not being collected. The producer appears only while a replay or smoke test runs.

panels.title: Errors and warnings (all programs)
panels.description: Every log line with the level error or warning, newest first. The processor logs the first ten alert lines of a replay as warnings.

panels.title: Follow one log line: type its ID in the box at the top
panels.description: Shows the log lines of all programs that contain the text typed in the box Trace ID. The smoke test sends one log line with a trace_id (the producer logs "sent") and the processor stores it with the same trace_id ("stored"). Oldest first, so you read its journey from top to bottom. With the box empty it shows all lines.
